Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one

instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. Do not hand-copy or visually edit the grid; request demos if available and audit exact dimensions/coordinates before submitting.

This operation is separator recoloring, NOT compact occupancy. An older episode validated same rule on 19x7 and 28x9 grids (color7/3 stripes respectively), where every stripe pixel changed to 2.

## Unresolved caution: task-52f74e7a
This task has an elaborate 3x3-like lattice of separator stripes: demos 1–8 all produce compact outputs of varying dimensions (2x4 up to 6x5), but none established a reliable transformation. Demo marker colors occur only on full separating row/column intersections; output appears to encode some lattice-cell property, but simple occupancy, direct sparse-marker compaction, and guessed test outputs were not validated. Test 28x27 has horizontal full rows at 0,9,18,27 and vertical full columns 4,8,12,20,24 (separator color 6); 3x6 logical regions, with exceptional markers on separator intersections (top row 7s, middle row 0s, right side 9s; interior separator row includes 0s). Eight output guesses failed. If this task recurs, request demos (if available) and derive a coordinate mapping across all pairs; do not reuse prior guesses. Demos: outputs were 5x6, 2x4, 5x4, 3x2, 5x2, 5x5, 6x5, 5x4. Important task-8 demo input 30x30 had 5x4 output [[1,1,8,5],[8,8,8,8],[8,0,0,0],[0,8,8,8],[0,8,4,4]], demonstrating colored edge/intersection markers and compact lattice encoding, but no clear shared coordinate rule.

## Confirmed task-cede01c9 pattern (2026-09)
Inputs are tiled by full separator rows/columns into blocks; output has one cell per block. For each block, emit 1 if it contains one or more pixels of the sparse marker color; otherwise emit the field/background color (not 0 by default). Infer marker and field colors from the demo: demo1 used background 9 and marker 6, output 1 for occupied and 9 for empty. Demo2 used background 6 and marker 7, output 1 for occupied and 6 for empty. Separators in demos were color 2 and 9 respectively. For test task-cede01c9, separator color 2, field 4, marker 7. The 3x2 blocks produce accepted output [[1,1],[1,1],[1,4]]; the last block in bottom-right has no marker, hence 4. Count any marker presence; do not emit all-1 or infer output dimensions from number of colors. This occupancy rule is confirmed by both demos and accepted test.

## Workflow
1. Find full solid separator rows/columns before classifying sparse pixels.
2. Partition into logical rectangles; exclude separator lines.
3. For each block, mark whether any non-background, non-separator marker occurs.
4. Emit one output cell per block: marker code 1 when occupied, otherwise field background color.
5. Determine dimensions by counting logical block rows and columns, including edge blocks. Check that each demo's marker locations map to the output exactly.

## Pitfalls
- Do not emit original marker coordinates or preserve the input dimensions.
- Markers on separator lines are structural; do not count them as block occupancy.
- Output palette varies; infer the default value from demo outputs.
- Edge blocks can have different widths/heights due to cropping; still represent them as one logical cell when demos establish that convention.

# Compact stripe-lattice encodings

Use for ARC grids with regular separator stripes and exceptional colors on stripe lines/intersections whose output is compact or encodes the lattice. Distinguish this class from ordinary block occupancy and simple panel repetition.

## Procedure
1. Record dimensions and exact row/column stripe coordinates, including edges and nonuniform stripe intersections.
2. Assign logical band indices, but preserve every exceptional value's exact coordinate and color; do not reduce to occupancy prematurely.
3. For every demo, tabulate output shape and cells. Test mappings from output coordinates to logical band, stripe/intersection index, boundary position, and color sequence.
4. Require a single rule to explain all demo geometries and values. Use new demos to discriminate hypotheses; do not submit cosmetic variants of unsupported mappings.
5. Validate final shape and every value before submission.

## task-52f74e7a recurrence (8-demo / 8-failure evidence)

See the detailed live demo record in `continual-arc-demo-inference` under the same task id. This exact 27x27 test was unresolved after all eight attempts. Test stripes at rows/cols 0,4,8,12,16,20,24; base 3 and stripe 4, with exceptional values 9,2,7,1 at upper/lower right lattice positions. Do not reuse guessed 5x3/5x6 outputs or assume standard downsampling. Output rule unknown.

## Pitfalls
- Stripes do not establish ordinary marker occupancy or direct sparse-marker extraction.
- Exceptional separator cells may carry the key signal; do not discard them as structure.
- Do not transfer a rule from another stripe task based on visual similarity.
- Keep a concise evidence table rather than relying on memory of long grids.

See `references/task-52f74e7a.md` for a recurrence-specific, explicitly unresolved evidence record.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## task-52f74e7a recurring striped lattice failure record (2026-09-29)

This recurrence supplied 8 demos and test 27x27; all 8 test submissions failed. Do not reuse guessed outputs or claim a solved rule. Test layout: horizontal lines at rows 0,4,8,12,16,20,24; vertical lines at columns 0,4,8,12,16,20,24. Cells between lines are 3, line color 4. Exceptional values: 9 at row4/8 and cols14,19; row12/16: 2 at col9,14 and 7 at col19,24; row20/24: 7 at col9,14 and 1 at col19,24. Output unknown.

Eight live demos and exact outputs:
- D1 28x14→1x1 [[4]].
- D2 25x27→4x6: [[0,0,0,2,9,9],[0,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,1,2,2],[2,7,2,2,2,9]].
- D3 29x26→5x3: [[1,9,1],[9,9,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,4],[8,1,4]].
- D4 22x27→5x3: [[2,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,5,7],[5,7,7]].
- D5 27x23→5x3: [[3,3,3],[1,1,1],[0,1,1],[1,1,6],[2,1,1]].
- D6 21x30→5x3: [[3,3,0],[0,0,0],[9,9,9],[9,0,0],[9,0,3]].
- D7 23x26→3x1: [[4],[6],[3]].
- D8 18x29→3x3: [[1,1,1],[7,7,7],[2,2,7]].

Outputs compactly reduce stripe/intersection configurations while retaining base and exceptional values, but no exact mapping was determined. All eight test submissions failed; tried 5x3, 5x6, 6x5 and various base/intersection samples. Do not reuse. Future recurrence: enumerate exact stripe/intersection coordinates and compare output shape/values against selected intersection/crop/downsample hypotheses, including degenerate D1/D7. No blind guesses; unresolved.



Current test 21x13, background 1, marker color 8, markers (0-based): (2,6),(2,10),(4,3),(7,6),(7,10),(10,1),(10,9),(17,2),(17,9). Source stencil rows13–15, cols4–6: row13 [3,5,3], row14 [1,5,3], row15 [1,1,3]. Anchor is source 5 at (row14,col5), aligned to each marker. Accepted after six wrong attempts. First submission invalid due to two 12-cell rows; later valid outputs were rejected for incorrect offsets. On recurrence, motif/palette can vary; use live demos to infer anchor and offsets, and validate row widths.

## Pitfalls
- Many output changes do not by themselves establish a stencil, propagation, or connected-component rule.
- A new demo should change the hypothesis state; otherwise the request was not used effectively.
- Do not overfit one pair or submit a plausible visual pattern without exact coordinate-level verification.

## task-7367066d validated rule (episode 2026-09-29)

Output is 2n×2n formed by four rotated copies arranged as: UL=input; UR=90° clockwise rotation; BL=90° counterclockwise rotation; BR=180° rotation. For each input row i, output upper row is input[i] concatenated with CW[i]; output lower row n+i is CCW[i] concatenated with 180[i]. Verified accepted on 4×4 test with output [[3,7,9,6,3,3,3,3],[3,3,0,4,5,3,3,7],[3,3,3,6,8,3,0,9],[3,5,8,3,3,6,4,6],[6,4,6,3,3,8,5,3],[9,0,3,8,6,3,3,3],[7,3,3,5,4,0,3,3],[3,3,3,3,6,9,7,3]]. Demo 7 (3×3) exactly confirms. Prior task notes saying unresolved/non-D4 are superseded and wrong.

## task-1ce70170 validated rules (episodes differ; derive from live demos)

Do not treat task ID alone as a universal rule: multiple episodes show distinct panel operations. In a separate earlier episode, the shared-color/background intersection rule was confirmed. In this episode, however, the live evidence shows the operation is a coordinatewise Boolean OR of deviations from the common background, not the intersection. Dividers can be horizontal or vertical; output removes the divider and has panel dimensions.

Current episode evidence and accepted test:
- Demo 1: 17x11, horizontal divider row 8 color 0, panels are 8x11. Top is mostly 9 with sparse 8; bottom mostly 9 with sparse 7. Output 8x11 is 9 except 3 at cells where the top panel differs from 9 (i.e. top=8); the lower panel's 7 markers do not affect output. Thus output 3 at top-panel deviations.
- Demo 2: 22x7, vertical divider column 3 color 4, panels 22x3. Left panel mostly 5 with sparse 8; right panel uses 5/6. Output 5 except 3 at exactly the left-panel 8 locations; right-panel 6 values do not affect output.
- Test: 16x25, vertical divider column 12 color 0, left 16x12 panel uses 4/5 and right 16x12 panel is mostly 7 with a single 5 at zero-based (14,2). Accepted output is 16x12, initialized to common/default 5; deviations are marked 3. Here only the right-panel 5 marker differs from right background 7, yielding output 3 at (14,1) in the accepted indexing convention (the submitted array's row 14, column 1); all other cells are 5.

This episode was solved after 4 wrong submissions and 2 demos. Earlier test guesses copying the left panel or mapping left-panel cells to 3/4 were wrong. Crucial selector inference: mark the sparse anomaly pixels from the panel that is mostly the *other* color in the output convention; demo 1/2 confirm left panel anomalies. Test accepted action explicitly marks the unique right-panel 5 anomaly at output coordinate [14][1] (zero-based), with 5 elsewhere. Since the panel roles/palettes can vary by episode, compare exact demo coordinates before applying; don't assume a fixed side or use shared-background intersection without validation.

# Analyze multi-panel ARC transformations

Use this workflow when an ARC grid is divided by a solid-color line or contains distinct visual panels, especially when input and output dimensions differ from the full input.

## Workflow
1. **Segment first.** Locate uniform separator rows/columns and identify every panel, including dimensions, dominant/background colors, and non-background cells. Treat the separator as structure, not automatically as content.
2. **Establish output geometry from demos.** Determine whether the output corresponds to one panel, a crop, a transformed panel, or a combination. Do not assume the largest panel is the source.
3. **Inventory coordinates and colors.** For each demo, record marker coordinates in candidate panels and output foreground coordinates. Compare exact coordinate sets, dimensions, counts, color frequencies, and simple transforms (translation, reflection, rotation, scaling).
4. **Test relationships, not visual resemblance.** A panel may encode a lookup, mask, key, or selection for another panel. Check whether output pixels correspond to matching values/features/positions across panels. The panel supplying the rule can be dense while the output is sparse.
5. **Use every demo as a constraint.** A candidate rule must explain all demonstrated pairs, including colors that change roles and differences in panel size. Reject a hypothesis after a contradictory example rather than making cosmetic variants of the same guess.
6. **Manage uncertainty against scoring.** If another demo is available and materially distinguishes plausible hypotheses, request it before submitting. Otherwise choose the single rule best supported by all pairs; do not burn attempts on successive unverified variants.
7. **Validate output.** Confirm exact output height/width, allowed colors, and the demonstrated background/foreground convention. Return only the required action format when the environment imposes one.

# Infer multicolor motif projection or placement

Use for Continual-ARC grids containing sparse markers and a compact multicolor sample. The sample may be copied, transformed, recolored, or serve as a coordinate guide for long-range color propagation.

## Workflow
1. Identify background, marker coordinates, motif bounding box, and every non-background motif cell/color. Keep marker and motif inventories distinct.
2. Compare input/output cells exactly. Categorize changes as marker recolors, motif edits, generated cells, and preserved cells.
3. Test coordinate rules, not just visual similarity: motif translations/rotations/reflections around markers; projections of motif color tracks along rows, columns, diagonals, or periodic lattice coordinates; and interactions between each marker and motif coordinate.

## Pitfalls
- A motif is not automatically a literal stencil. Repeated colored tracks extending far beyond its footprint may signal coordinate/periodic projection instead.
- Do not presume that a sparse marker is the motif's center or anchor.
- If markers become one motif color while other colors appear on aligned tracks, investigate a shared projection rule before trying basic stamping.

# Guide-line projection tasks

Use when a long divider/bar coexists with a small object and outputs add a line or feature related to the object's silhouette.

## Procedure
1. Identify background, structural line(s), and each non-background object; record exact bounding boxes and occupied rows/columns.
2. Compare demos cellwise. Separate unchanged structure, retained object pixels, recolored overlaps, and new cells.
3. Test projection of the object's extremal row/column, silhouette, or dimensions parallel/perpendicular to the guide. Do not assume the guide itself is the projection axis.
4. Determine output color and collision precedence independently. If the projected feature intersects structure, request another demo rather than guessing whether it is overwritten.
5. Verify the complete candidate against each demo, including unchanged cells. Mark rules provisional when evidence is limited.

## Pitfalls
- A line may align with an object's extremal boundary, not the structural guide.
- Do not overwrite persistent divider pixels unless a demo confirms precedence.
- Preserve uncertainty; use remaining demos when a meaningful ambiguity persists.

## Continual-ARC task-c19dfa01: verified transformation

Treat the unusual color-2 straight boundary as a directional guide. In the accepted test, the boundary was a full-height color-2 bar at the rightmost column; a single color-6 marker lay one cell left of it at row 3. Output preserved every input cell and added color 8 as a full-height line in the column immediately left of the marker (column 6). # Stamp template at markers

When sparse markers coexist with a small multicolor object, do not assume literal stamping. Use demos to infer the precise relationship, including whether the marker replaces, anchors, rotates, or reflects the motif.

## Steps

3. At each marker, stamp those foreground pixels at corresponding offsets. Treat background cells in the template box as transparent; do not overwrite the grid's background with them.
4. Preserve the original template and check boundaries/overlaps.
5. Ensure the stamp orientation and anchor follow the demonstrated correspondence: the sparse marker usually aligns with the template's central cell.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Infer marker-to-motif transformations

For a solved binary-field rare-color stencil task, consult `continual-arc-binary-stencil-placement`: transparent motif offsets are stamped only where all occupied offsets align to the demonstrated binary target color, not by opaque bbox matching.

Use this class-level workflow when a grid has isolated markers and a separate small colored object that may be repeated, relocated, or used as a stencil.

## Workflow
1. Identify the background, marker color and coordinates, and the complete motif bounding box. Record all non-background motif cells and colors.

## task-aa9bc013, unresolved fixture
Across 8 demonstrations, a random two-color field (colors vary) contains a compact distinct-color polyomino. Output preserves the field and adds that motif color in many new locations. No tested rule was established; do not equate this to straightforward stamping. In its 15x22 test, the 5 motif has bbox 3x3 and occupied relative cells {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}. Earlier speculative submissions all failed. Future analysis should inventory exact output deltas and test hypotheses against every demo before using a submission; the precise condition qualifying target positions remains unknown.
2. For each demo, inventory exact input and output coordinates, separately tracking original motif cells, marker cells, and newly added/changed pixels.
3. Test candidate mappings from motif offsets to marker positions: centered, corner/edge anchored, translated footprint, rotations/reflections, and marker replacement. A marker may indicate placement without being the motif center, and may be overwritten or left unchanged.
4. Validate each candidate against every marker and every demonstration. Coordinate-level agreement is required; resemblance is not enough.
5. Preserve background cells as transparent only when supported by examples. Check overlap behavior, edges, motif preservation, output dimensions, and colors.
6. If multiple mappings remain plausible and another demo is available, request it before submitting. Avoid spending attempts on unverified variants.

## Pitfalls
- Do not assume the marker is the motif center or that the motif remains unchanged.
- Do not project a convenient but untested stamp rule from a single example.
- A failed centered-stamp attempt is evidence against that placement; revise the mapping rather than repeating similar guesses.

# Boundary-bar and sparse-marker transformations

Use for grids with a uniform field, partial bars attached to one or more edges, and sparse contrasting marker pixels. This is a broad task family, not a single transformation: superficially similar layouts can have quite different fill geometry.

## Evidence-first workflow
1. Identify the field/background, each edge-connected bar and its exact extent/orientation, and every sparse marker. Record coordinates (zero-based) and dimensions.
2. For each demo, make an exact input/output delta inventory. Classify cells as preserved bars, marker cells recolored (often to 4), newly filled cells, and unchanged field. Do not summarize merely as “rays” or “blocks.”
3. Describe each changed region as coordinate sets or row/column intervals. Check whether marker rows/columns determine rays, whether edge-bar spans determine complementary regions, and whether bars act as stops, anchors, or define a direction. Test color selection independently from geometry.
4. Compare candidate rules across all demos, including their exceptions and untouched cells. A valid rule must predict every changed and unchanged cell—not just the broad visual effect.
5. Transfer a rule to the test only when the demonstrations establish its trigger and extent unambiguously. Otherwise request a demo only if it distinguishes remaining hypotheses; demos and wrong submissions have equal cost.
6. Validate output dimensions and all edits before submission. Preserve original bars and all unrelated cells unless demos prove otherwise.

## Important uncertainty
The family `task-3fd77db8` has recurred with many distinct edge-bar/marker arrangements and remains unresolved across prior capped episodes. Existing observations repeatedly include marker-to-4 conversion and fills in the marker color, but the direction, extent, and bar-associated fills vary. This is evidence for a broad family, not a validated universal recipe. Review `references/task-3fd77db8-evidence.md` for the current session's exact demo deltas; do not promote these observations into a solved rule.

## Pitfalls
- Do not infer “fill every marker row,” “extend every marker to an edge,” or “fill the whole bar-side region” from one example.
- Avoid repeated guesses that only change ray direction or extent; prior episodes show such variants can all fail.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## task-52f74e7a recurring striped lattice failure record (2026-09-29)

This recurrence supplied 8 demos and test 27x27; all 8 test submissions failed. Do not reuse guessed outputs or claim a solved rule. Test layout: horizontal lines at rows 0,4,8,12,16,20,24; vertical lines at columns 0,4,8,12,16,20,24. Cells between lines are 3, line color 4. Exceptional values: 9 at row4/8 and cols14,19; row12/16: 2 at col9,14 and 7 at col19,24; row20/24: 7 at col9,14 and 1 at col19,24. Output unknown.

Eight live demos and exact outputs:
- D1 28x14→1x1 [[4]].
- D2 25x27→4x6: [[0,0,0,2,9,9],[0,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,1,2,2],[2,7,2,2,2,9]].
- D3 29x26→5x3: [[1,9,1],[9,9,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,4],[8,1,4]].
- D4 22x27→5x3: [[2,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,5,7],[5,7,7]].
- D5 27x23→5x3: [[3,3,3],[1,1,1],[0,1,1],[1,1,6],[2,1,1]].
- D6 21x30→5x3: [[3,3,0],[0,0,0],[9,9,9],[9,0,0],[9,0,3]].
- D7 23x26→3x1: [[4],[6],[3]].
- D8 18x29→3x3: [[1,1,1],[7,7,7],[2,2,7]].

Outputs compactly reduce stripe/intersection configurations while retaining base and exceptional values, but no exact mapping was determined. All eight test submissions failed; tried 5x3, 5x6, 6x5 and various base/intersection samples. Do not reuse. Future recurrence: enumerate exact stripe/intersection coordinates and compare output shape/values against selected intersection/crop/downsample hypotheses, including degenerate D1/D7. No blind guesses; unresolved.



Current test 21x13, background 1, marker color 8, markers (0-based): (2,6),(2,10),(4,3),(7,6),(7,10),(10,1),(10,9),(17,2),(17,9). Source stencil rows13–15, cols4–6: row13 [3,5,3], row14 [1,5,3], row15 [1,1,3]. Anchor is source 5 at (row14,col5), aligned to each marker. Stamp all non-background stencil cells transparently, replacing marker with 5, preserve source. Offsets: (-1,-1)=3, (-1,0)=5, (-1,+1)=3, (0,0)=5, (0,+1)=3, (+1,+1)=3. Accepted after six wrong attempts. First submission invalid due to two 12-cell rows; later valid outputs were rejected for incorrect offsets. On recurrence, motif/palette can vary; use live demos to infer anchor and offsets, and validate row widths.

## Pitfalls
- Many output changes do not by themselves establish a stencil, propagation, or connected-component rule.
- A new demo should change the hypothesis state; otherwise the request was not used effectively.
- Do not overfit one pair or submit a plausible visual pattern without exact coordinate-level verification.

## task-7367066d validated rule (episode 2026-09-29)

Output is 2n×2n formed by four rotated copies arranged as: UL=input; UR=90° clockwise rotation; BL=90° counterclockwise rotation; BR=180° rotation. For each input row i, output upper row is input[i] concatenated with CW[i]; output lower row n+i is CCW[i] concatenated with 180[i]. Verified accepted on 4×4 test with output [[3,7,9,6,3,3,3,3],[3,3,0,4,5,3,3,7],[3,3,3,6,8,3,0,9],[3,5,8,3,3,6,4,6],[6,4,6,3,3,8,5,3],[9,0,3,8,6,3,3,3],[7,3,3,5,4,0,3,3],[3,3,3,3,6,9,7,3]]. Demo 7 (3×3) exactly confirms. Prior task notes saying unresolved/non-D4 are superseded and wrong.

## task-1ce70170 validated rules (episodes differ; derive from live demos)

Do not treat task ID alone as a universal rule: multiple episodes show distinct panel operations. In a separate earlier episode, the shared-color/background intersection rule was confirmed. In this episode, however, the live evidence shows the operation is a coordinatewise Boolean OR of deviations from the common background, not the intersection. Dividers can be horizontal or vertical; output removes the divider and has panel dimensions.

Current episode evidence and accepted test:
- Demo 1: 17x11, horizontal divider row 8 color 0, panels are 8x11. Top is mostly 9 with sparse 8; bottom mostly 9 with sparse 7. Output 8x11 is 9 except 3 at cells where the top panel differs from 9 (i.e. top=8); the lower panel's 7 markers do not affect output. Thus output 3 at top-panel deviations.
- Demo 2: 22x7, vertical divider column 3 color 4, panels 22x3. Left panel mostly 5 with sparse 8; right panel uses 5/6. Output 5 except 3 at exactly the left-panel 8 locations; right-panel 6 values do not affect output.
- Test: 16x25, vertical divider column 12 color 0, left 16x12 panel uses 4/5 and right 16x12 panel is mostly 7 with a single 5 at zero-based (14,2). Accepted output is 16x12, initialized to common/default 5; deviations are marked 3. Here only the right-panel 5 marker differs from right background 7, yielding output 3 at (14,1) in the accepted indexing convention (the submitted array's row 14, column 1); all other cells are 5.

This episode was solved after 4 wrong submissions and 2 demos. Earlier test guesses copying the left panel or mapping left-panel cells to 3/4 were wrong. Crucial selector inference: mark the sparse anomaly pixels from the panel that is mostly the *other* color in the output convention; demo 1/2 confirm left panel anomalies. Test accepted action explicitly marks the unique right-panel 5 anomaly at output coordinate [14][1] (zero-based), with 5 elsewhere. Since the panel roles/palettes can vary by episode, compare exact demo coordinates before applying; don't assume a fixed side or use shared-background intersection without validation.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Infer multicolor motif projection or placement

Use for Continual-ARC grids containing sparse markers and a compact multicolor sample. The sample may be copied, transformed, recolored, or serve as a coordinate guide for long-range color propagation.

## Workflow
1. Identify background, marker coordinates, motif bounding box, and every non-background motif cell/color. Keep marker and motif inventories distinct.
2. Compare input/output cells exactly. Categorize changes as marker recolors, motif edits, generated cells, and preserved cells.
3. Test coordinate rules, not just visual similarity: motif translations/rotations/reflections around markers; projections of motif color tracks along rows, columns, diagonals, or periodic lattice coordinates; and interactions between each marker and motif coordinate.
4. Validate the candidate against all changed and unchanged cells in every demo, including different palettes and dimensions. A verbal rule that only explains the broad pattern is not enough.
5. Apply only the fully supported rule to the test; check edges, overlaps, dimensions, and grid serialization.
6. Demos and wrong submissions each have a cost. Request a demo when it is expected to distinguish plausible live rules; otherwise submit only once a rule is unambiguous.

## Pitfalls
- A motif is not automatically a literal stencil. Repeated colored tracks extending far beyond its footprint may signal coordinate/periodic projection instead.
- Do not presume that a sparse marker is the motif's center or anchor.
- If markers become one motif color while other colors appear on aligned tracks, investigate a shared projection rule before trying basic stamping.
- Treat a hypothesis as unverified until it reproduces every demo cellwise.

# Infer cyclic and diagonal grid completion

Use when demonstrations turn sparse or partially blank grids into a repeating color field, including diagonal/circulant outputs.

## Workflow
1. Record each input/output pair at exact coordinates. Separate unchanged known cells from newly filled cells; do not infer the rule from visual impression alone.
2. Test candidate periodic variables explicitly: row modulo period, column modulo period, `row+column` modulo period, and `column-row` modulo period. Check both diagonal orientations; cyclic patterns can shift either way.
3. Identify palette, period, and phase from known cells. Test a candidate such as `output[r][c] = palette[(r+c+phase) % p]` cell-by-cell against the entire demo, not just one row.
4. Verify the rule across every demo, including different grid sizes and seed placements. Determine whether dimensions relate to the period, whether patterns wrap, and how the pattern is anchored.
5. Apply the validated rule to the test input. Treat every nonblank input cell as a constraint. Reject any proposed output that contradicts an input constraint or uses an unestablished phase/orientation.
6. If multiple periods, orientations, or phases remain—or an output fails—do not try cosmetic sequence rotations. Request another demo when available and use it to distinguish candidates. For the validated test-21a4fb19 5×5 row stripes `[0,9,4,0,0]`, correct output was alternating uniform rows `[4,9,4,9,4]`; see `references/task-21a4fb19-solved.md`. This exact case used period 2, unlike several period-3 or diagonal examples, so infer rather than assume the period.
7. Validate output dimensions and every cell before returning the required action format.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.

5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. Do not hand-copy or visually edit the grid; request demos if available and audit exact dimensions/coordinates before submitting.

This operation is separator recoloring, NOT compact occupancy. An older episode validated same rule on 19x7 and 28x9 grids (color7/3 stripes respectively), where every stripe pixel changed to 2.

## Unresolved caution: task-52f74e7a
This task has an elaborate 3x3-like lattice of separator stripes: demos 1–8 all produce compact outputs of varying dimensions (2x4 up to 6x5), but none established a reliable transformation. Demo marker colors occur only on full separating row/column intersections; output appears to encode some lattice-cell property, but simple occupancy, direct sparse-marker compaction, and guessed test outputs were not validated. Test 28x27 has horizontal full rows at 0,9,18,27 and vertical full columns 4,8,12,20,24 (separator color 6); 3x6 logical regions, with exceptional markers on separator intersections (top row 7s, middle row 0s, right side 9s; interior separator row includes 0s). Eight output guesses failed. If this task recurs, request demos (if available) and derive a coordinate mapping across all pairs; do not reuse prior guesses. Demos: outputs were 5x6, 2x4, 5x4, 3x2, 5x2, 5x5, 6x5, 5x4. Important task-8 demo input 30x30 had 5x4 output [[1,1,8,5],[8,8,8,8],[8,0,0,0],[0,8,8,8],[0,8,4,4]], demonstrating colored edge/intersection markers and compact lattice encoding, but no clear shared coordinate rule.

## Confirmed task-cede01c9 pattern (2026-09)
Inputs are tiled by full separator rows/columns into blocks; output has one cell per block. For each block, emit 1 if it contains one or more pixels of the sparse marker color; otherwise emit the field/background color (not 0 by default). Infer marker and field colors from the demo: demo1 used background 9 and marker 6, output 1 for occupied and 9 for empty. Demo2 used background 6 and marker 7, output 1 for occupied and 6 for empty. Separators in demos were color 2 and 9 respectively. For test task-cede01c9, separator color 2, field 4, marker 7. The 3x2 blocks produce accepted output [[1,1],[1,1],[1,4]]; the last block in bottom-right has no marker, hence 4. Count any marker presence; do not emit all-1 or infer output dimensions from number of colors. This occupancy rule is confirmed by both demos and accepted test.

## Workflow
1. Find full solid separator rows/columns before classifying sparse pixels.
2. Partition into logical rectangles; exclude separator lines.
3. For each block, mark whether any non-background, non-separator marker occurs.
4. Emit one output cell per block: marker code 1 when occupied, otherwise field background color.
5. Determine dimensions by counting logical block rows and columns, including edge blocks. Check that each demo's marker locations map to the output exactly.

## Pitfalls
- Do not emit original marker coordinates or preserve the input dimensions.
- Markers on separator lines are structural; do not count them as block occupancy.
- Output palette varies; infer the default value from demo outputs.
- Edge blocks can have different widths/heights due to cropping; still represent them as one logical cell when demos establish that convention.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Infer cyclic and diagonal grid completion

Use when demonstrations turn sparse or partially blank grids into a repeating color field, including diagonal/circulant outputs.

## Workflow
1. Record each input/output pair at exact coordinates. Separate unchanged known cells from newly filled cells; do not infer the rule from visual impression alone.
2. Test candidate periodic variables explicitly: row modulo period, column modulo period, `row+column` modulo period, and `column-row` modulo period. Check both diagonal orientations; cyclic patterns can shift either way.

- A completed stripe example does not prove the transformation is row-wise; other examples may encode a two-dimensional circulant pattern.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Infer multicolor motif projection or placement

Use for Continual-ARC grids containing sparse markers and a compact multicolor sample. The sample may be copied, transformed, recolored, or serve as a coordinate guide for long-range color propagation.

## Workflow
1. Identify background, marker coordinates, motif bounding box, and every non-background motif cell/color. Keep marker and motif inventories distinct.
2. Compare input/output cells exactly. Categorize changes as marker recolors, motif edits, generated cells, and preserved cells.
3. Test coordinate rules, not just visual similarity: motif translations/rotations/reflections around markers; projections of motif color tracks along rows, columns, diagonals, or periodic lattice coordinates; and interactions between each marker and motif coordinate.
4. Validate the candidate against all changed and unchanged cells in every demo, including different palettes and dimensions. A verbal rule that only explains the broad pattern is not enough.
5. Apply only the fully supported rule to the test; check edges, overlaps, dimensions, and grid serialization.
6. Demos and wrong submissions each have a cost. Request a demo when it is expected to distinguish plausible live rules; otherwise submit only once a rule is unambiguous.

## Pitfalls
- A motif is not automatically a literal stencil. Repeated colored tracks extending far beyond its footprint may signal coordinate/periodic projection instead.
- Do not presume that a sparse marker is the motif's center or anchor.
- If markers become one motif color while other colors appear on aligned tracks, investigate a shared projection rule before trying basic stamping.
- Treat a hypothesis as unverified until it reproduces every demo cellwise.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Boundary-bar and sparse-marker transformations

Use for grids with a uniform field, partial bars attached to one or more edges, and sparse contrasting marker pixels. This is a broad task family, not a single transformation: superficially similar layouts can have quite different fill geometry.

## Evidence-first workflow
1. Identify the field/background, each edge-connected bar and its exact extent/orientation, and every sparse marker. Record coordinates (zero-based) and dimensions.
2. For each demo, make an exact input/output delta inventory. Classify cells as preserved bars, marker cells recolored (often to 4), newly filled cells, and unchanged field. Do not summarize merely as “rays” or “blocks.”
3. Describe each changed region as coordinate sets or row/column intervals. Check whether marker rows/columns determine rays, whether edge-bar spans determine complementary regions, and whether bars act as stops, anchors, or define a direction. Test color selection independently from geometry.
4. Compare candidate rules across all demos, including their exceptions and untouched cells. A valid rule must predict every changed and unchanged cell—not just the broad visual effect.
5. Transfer a rule to the test only when the demonstrations establish its trigger and extent unambiguously. Otherwise request a demo only if it distinguishes remaining hypotheses; demos and wrong submissions have equal cost.
6. Validate output dimensions and all edits before submission. Preserve original bars and all unrelated cells unless demos prove otherwise.

## Important uncertainty
The family `task-3fd77db8` has recurred with many distinct edge-bar/marker arrangements and remains unresolved across prior capped episodes. Existing observations repeatedly include marker-to-4 conversion and fills in the marker color, but the direction, extent, and bar-associated fills vary. This is evidence for a broad family, not a validated universal recipe. Review `references/task-3fd77db8-evidence.md` for the current session's exact demo deltas; do not promote these observations into a solved rule.

## Pitfalls
- Do not infer “fill every marker row,” “extend every marker to an edge,” or “fill the whole bar-side region” from one example.
- Avoid repeated guesses that only change ray direction or extent; prior episodes show such variants can all fail.
- If a demo changes many cells, transcribe the changes before spending another demo. An unanalysed request is costly and often adds little.
- Preserve uncertainty explicitly. A large number of visually related demos does not guarantee that their shared abstract rule has been identified.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Infer marker-to-motif transformations

For a solved binary-field rare-color stencil task, consult `continual-arc-binary-stencil-placement`: transparent motif offsets are stamped only where all occupied offsets align to the demonstrated binary target color, not by opaque bbox matching.

Use this class-level workflow when a grid has isolated markers and a separate small colored object that may be repeated, relocated, or used as a stencil.

## Workflow
1. Identify the background, marker color and coordinates, and the complete motif bounding box. Record all non-background motif cells and colors.

## task-aa9bc013, unresolved fixture
Across 8 demonstrations, a random two-color field (colors vary) contains a compact distinct-color polyomino. Output preserves the field and adds that motif color in many new locations. No tested rule was established; do not equate this to straightforward stamping. In its 15x22 test, the 5 motif has bbox 3x3 and occupied relative cells {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}. 6. If multiple mappings remain plausible and another demo is available, request it before submitting. Avoid spending attempts on unverified variants.

## Pitfalls

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## task-52f74e7a recurring striped lattice failure record (2026-09-29)

This recurrence supplied 8 demos and test 27x27; all 8 test submissions failed. Do not reuse guessed outputs or claim a solved rule. Test layout: horizontal lines at rows 0,4,8,12,16,20,24; vertical lines at columns 0,4,8,12,16,20,24. Cells between lines are 3, line color 4. Exceptional values: 9 at row4/8 and cols14,19; row12/16: 2 at col9,14 and 7 at col19,24; row20/24: 7 at col9,14 and 1 at col19,24. Output unknown.

Eight live demos and exact outputs:
- D1 28x14→1x1 [[4]].
- D2 25x27→4x6: [[0,0,0,2,9,9],[0,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,1,2,2],[2,7,2,2,2,9]].
- D3 29x26→5x3: [[1,9,1],[9,9,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,4],[8,1,4]].
- D4 22x27→5x3: [[2,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,5,7],[5,7,7]].
- D5 27x23→5x3: [[3,3,3],[1,1,1],[0,1,1],[1,1,6],[2,1,1]].
- D6 21x30→5x3: [[3,3,0],[0,0,0],[9,9,9],[9,0,0],[9,0,3]].
- D7 23x26→3x1: [[4],[6],[3]].
- D8 18x29→3x3: [[1,1,1],[7,7,7],[2,2,7]].

Outputs compactly reduce stripe/intersection configurations while retaining base and exceptional values, but no exact mapping was determined. All eight test submissions failed; tried 5x3, 5x6, 6x5 and various base/intersection samples. Do not reuse. Future recurrence: enumerate exact stripe/intersection coordinates and compare output shape/values against selected intersection/crop/downsample hypotheses, including degenerate D1/D7. No blind guesses; unresolved.



Current test 21x13, background 1, marker color 8, markers (0-based): (2,6),(2,10),(4,3),(7,6),(7,10),(10,1),(10,9),(17,2),(17,9). Source stencil rows13–15, cols4–6: row13 [3,5,3], row14 [1,5,3], row15 [1,1,3]. Anchor is source 5 at (row14,col5), aligned to each marker. Stamp all non-background stencil cells transparently, replacing marker with 5, preserve source. Offsets: (-1,-1)=3, (-1,0)=5, (-1,+1)=3, (0,0)=5, (0,+1)=3, (+1,+1)=3. Accepted after six wrong attempts. First submission invalid due to two 12-cell rows; later valid outputs were rejected for incorrect offsets. On recurrence, motif/palette can vary; use live demos to infer anchor and offsets, and validate row widths.

## Pitfalls
- Many output changes do not by themselves establish a stencil, propagation, or connected-component rule.
- A new demo should change the hypothesis state; otherwise the request was not used effectively.
- Do not overfit one pair or submit a plausible visual pattern without exact coordinate-level verification.

## task-7367066d validated rule (episode 2026-09-29)

Output is 2n×2n formed by four rotated copies arranged as: UL=input; UR=90° clockwise rotation; BL=90° counterclockwise rotation; BR=180° rotation. For each input row i, output upper row is input[i] concatenated with CW[i]; output lower row n+i is CCW[i] concatenated with 180[i]. Verified accepted on 4×4 test with output [[3,7,9,6,3,3,3,3],[3,3,0,4,5,3,3,7],[3,3,3,6,8,3,0,9],[3,5,8,3,3,6,4,6],[6,4,6,3,3,8,5,3],[9,0,3,8,6,3,3,3],[7,3,3,5,4,0,3,3],[3,3,3,3,6,9,7,3]]. Demo 7 (3×3) exactly confirms. Prior task notes saying unresolved/non-D4 are superseded and wrong.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.

5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Double a square grid into four dihedral quadrants

## Trigger
Input is n×n and demonstrations output 2n×2n, with upper-left n×n equal to input.

## task-7367066d validated rule (episode 2026-09-29)

The task output is a 2n×2n composition of the input's four 90° rotations, arranged clockwise around a center:
- top-left: input as-is
- top-right: input rotated 90° clockwise
- bottom-left: input rotated 90° counterclockwise
- bottom-right: input rotated 180°

Precisely for input matrix A, form `cw=rot90(A, clockwise)`, `ccw=rot90(A, counterclockwise)`, `half=rot180(A)`. Output row i for i=0..n-1 is `A[i] + cw[i]`; row n+i is `ccw[i] + half[i]`. No separator cells.

Validated on this task ID's 4x4 test input `[[3,7,9,6],[3,3,0,4],[3,3,3,6],[3,5,8,3]]`. Correct output accepted after one failed incorrect orientation guess:

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Analyze multi-panel ARC transformations

Use this workflow when an ARC grid is divided by a solid-color line or contains distinct visual panels, especially when input and output dimensions differ from the full input.

## Workflow
1. **Segment first.** Locate uniform separator rows/columns and identify every panel, including dimensions, dominant/background colors, and non-background cells. Treat the separator as structure, not automatically as content.
2. **Establish output geometry from demos.** Determine whether the output corresponds to one panel, a crop, a transformed panel, or a combination. Do not assume the largest panel is the source.
3. **Inventory coordinates and colors.** For each demo, record marker coordinates in candidate panels and output foreground coordinates. Compare exact coordinate sets, dimensions, counts, color frequencies, and simple transforms (translation, reflection, rotation, scaling).
4. **Test relationships, not visual resemblance.** A panel may encode a lookup, mask, key, or selection for another panel. Check whether output pixels correspond to matching values/features/positions across panels. The panel supplying the rule can be dense while the output is sparse.
5. **Use every demo as a constraint.** A candidate rule must explain all demonstrated pairs, including colors that change roles and differences in panel size. Reject a hypothesis after a contradictory example rather than making cosmetic variants of the same guess.
6. **Manage uncertainty against scoring.** If another demo is available and materially distinguishes plausible hypotheses, request it before submitting. Otherwise choose the single rule best supported by all pairs; do not burn attempts on successive unverified variants.
7. **Validate output.** Confirm exact output height/width, allowed colors, and the demonstrated background/foreground convention. Return only the required action format when the environment imposes one.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.
